title: Glacial Loss and Threatened Fish: The Future of Mount Rainier's Cold‐Water Bull Trout Habitats
content:
ABSTRACT

Rivers supplied by glacial ice provide critical habitat for aquatic organisms that survive only in cold water, including federally threatened Bull Trout (Salvelinus confluentus). However, as glaciers retreat due to climate change, stream temperatures in key habitats could warm. This issue is particularly relevant to heavily glaciated Mount Rainier (Washington State, USA), where rivers sourced from cold glacial meltwater provide crucial spawning habitats for Bull Trout. To explore current and future conditions in these habitats, we used stream temperature data collected in the glacially fed White and Carbon Rivers to build spatial stream network models, representing contemporary thermal conditions as a function of glacial extent and air temperature. We focused predictions on Bull Trout spawning season, using September 7-day average daily maximum (7DADM) stream temperatures. To simulate future climate change impacts, we adjusted models to predict stream temperature in mid- and late-century scenarios of air temperature rise and decreased glacial extent. The average 7DADM temperature predicted for contemporary conditions was 6.3°C and 8.1°C in the White and Carbon River watersheds, respectively. With higher air temperatures and smaller glaciers, stream temperatures warmed by up to 9.4°C in the White River and 4.6°C in the Carbon by late century. The future proportion of thermally viable habitat for Bull Trout spawning significantly declined in both watersheds. Predictions for specific spawning streams, however, found that a few locations may continue to provide cold conditions. These results and methods can be utilized in the conservation of sensitive species and their enduring habitats in glacial rivers.
